Title: Foods That Make Rhinitis Worse (3 Everyday Triggers)

Description:
Taking allergy medicine every day but still waking up mouth-breathing? Some everyday foods raise histamine or inflammation in the body, and that can make sneezing, congestion, and a runny nose worse.

Dairy, wine and alcohol, and cured meats or aged cheese are common culprits - each one has a simple swap that doesn't mean cutting it out for good.

Watch to find out why, and what to try instead.

platforms.title: Nose Reacting to Wine, Cheese, or Spicy Food? Here's Why
platforms.meta_description: Nasal congestion after wine, aged cheese, or spicy food isn't always allergies. Histamine and capsaicin both irritate the nose - here's what actually helps.
platforms.body_html:
Reaching for a tissue after a glass of wine, a slice of aged cheese, or a spicy meal isn't always a coincidence, and it isn't always classic allergies either. Two different, well-documented reactions can make the nose run or feel blocked right after eating: histamine intolerance triggered by certain foods, and a nerve reflex set off by spicy or piping-hot dishes. Here's what's actually behind each one, and what tends to help.

Histamine-Rich Foods: Aged Cheese, Cured Meats, and Wine

Histamine is a natural compound the body produces, but it's also present in food, and some foods carry a lot of it. Aged cheeses, cured meats like salami and prosciutto, and wine (especially red) build up histamine during fermentation and aging. An enzyme called DAO (diamine oxidase) normally breaks down histamine from food in the gut. When DAO activity can't keep pace, whether from a temporary imbalance or an ongoing sensitivity, the extra histamine can trigger sneezing, a stuffy or runny nose, flushing, and headaches, usually within a couple of hours of eating. Combining several histamine-rich foods in one sitting, like a cheese board with red wine and salami, tends to make the reaction more noticeable than eating just one.

Spicy Food and a Nerve Reflex, Not an Allergy

A runny nose partway through a spicy or very hot meal has a different explanation: gustatory rhinitis. Capsaicin, the compound that makes chili peppers hot, activates heat- and pain-sensing nerve receptors (TRPV1) in the mouth and nose. Those nerves connect to the same reflex that controls the nose's mucus glands, so the body responds by producing extra mucus to help flush out the irritant, even though nothing is actually wrong. This reflex is thought to affect a meaningful share of adults and has nothing to do with the immune system, unlike a true allergy.

What Actually Helps

  • Skip the cheese-and-wine combo — Aged cheese, cured meat, and red wine are each high in histamine on their own; stacking them in one meal is usually what pushes symptoms over the edge.
  • Choose fresher, less-aged options — Fresh mozzarella or ricotta carries far less histamine than a hard aged cheese, and white wine tends to contain less than red.
  • Let hot food cool slightly — A few extra minutes before the first bite gives the nerve reflex less to react to.
  • Space out trigger foods — Eating them apart instead of back to back gives your body more time to process histamine before the next dose arrives.

The Bottom Line

Neither of these reactions means something is seriously wrong, and neither food group needs to disappear from your plate for good. Paying attention to which combinations set off symptoms, and easing up on those specific pairings, is usually enough. This article is for general information only and isn't medical advice; if congestion is frequent, severe, or comes with other symptoms, it's worth checking with an allergist or ENT doctor.
